items.title: Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture
items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension.  Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification.  For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. items.title: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now Here’s a speech I gave on Saturday the 17th of October at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. While we all may quibble over the details, I think it’s evident we’re in the early stages of the singularity, and I wanted to use my privileged position of giving the Per Jacobsson lecture to try and tell the assembled audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers, that they should expect significant, rapid change in the future. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues. As I said a few times in the speech – some of which was ad libbed and not captured here – I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. I find myself both a narrator of what is happening in AI, a principle agent behind what is happening in AI, and a translator that goes between many communities. In all of this, I am seeking to be truthful and to be clear about my own culpability. This is a forever work-in-progress. Thank you all for reading. Speeches like this draw heavily from the newsletter, and the newsletter is my attempt to provide week-by-week information to all of you. I appreciate your readership. *** Inside the Event Horizon: Why Everyone Should Take AI Progress Seriously Hello, thank you for having me. It is a great privilege to be here. To start, I should list my relevant credentials: I am a human being. There is one of me. It has taken me almost 40 years to build the experience to give this speech. I will come back to those credentials late…

items.title: You are the Team — Anekha Sokhal, Moshi
items.content: Tickets and applications now live for AIE CODE - the last flagship AIE of the year. When Anekha Sokhal traded energy derivatives, staying on top of the market meant tracking more information than any person could read. Now, as CEO of Moshi, she is building the tool she wished she had: a recommendation engine that connects market information to what matters for a trader’s book. At AI Engineer New York, Anekha joins swyx to discuss her path from mathematics and JPMorgan to founding Moshi, and why useful AI needs to fit the way people actually work. She describes Moshi as what might happen if Bloomberg, Claude and Netflix had a baby: market data, an interface for working with it, and recommendations tailored to the trader. They also talk about trusted sources, document extraction, building versus buying models, and the pressure on AI engineers who are told, “you are the team.” Anekha shares what she learned from customer conversations at the conference and why meeting users comes before hiring. items.title: Take Ten-Thousand: Egocentric Data Collection for Humanoid Robots
items.content: The ChinaTalk team is going to CoRL (the Conference on Robot Learning) in Austin! Reply to this email if you’d like to hang out between November 9th and 12th. We’re also doing karaoke on the 11th — RSVP here if you’d like to join! A. Chen writes about people, technologies, and their relationships to power. Her submission, “Take Ten-Thousand: Egocentric Data Collection for Humanoid Robots,” won one of 7 Grand Prizes at the ChinaTalk Essay Contest. We’re thrilled to share this report from the frontlines of China’s robot data collection industry! Where is the center of the universe? For the residents of Beijing, the answer is Wudaokou. The neighborhood houses China’s top universities, research institutions, and labs, drawing talent and funding from every corner of the country. The streets are radiant at night, packed full of bars and clubs that have somehow bounced back after the COVID-19 pandemic. And the number 13 metro line, which rattles overhead every five minutes, is never empty. I came to Wudaokou to understand China’s AI industry — particularly, the hype surrounding humanoid robots, and the methods used to train them. Everyone has seen videos of these robots: eerily tall and lanky, some of them shedding nuts and bolts as they sprint down a track, others backflipping repeatedly on a dance stage. The global market for humanoid robotics, or embodied intelligence, is said to be worth $38 billion by 2035: the latest chapter in the U.S.-China technology race that has dominated international headlines for over a decade. This year, China’s 15 th Five-Year Plan declared embodied intelligence a matter of national priority, then laid a strategy for developing training grounds across the country. Over 150 humanoid robotics companies and 40 state-owned robot data collection centers were reported to be in operation in China by the end of 2025. items.title: MOFCOM's New Rules and the Future of Chinese AI
items.content: In the AI race thus far, openness has been China’s secret sauce. As fast followers to the frontier, Chinese AI companies have gained trust by publicizing their weights and architectures. And at the cost of revenue, they have achieved global adoption, brand recognition, and a truly competitive dynamic with American labs. Last week, China’s Ministries of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Science and Technology (MOST) jointly proposed expanding China’s catalogue of export-controlled technologies, with most of the proposed regulations taking aim at subsets of China’s AI industry. Regulators will spend a month taking comments on the draft before anything becomes law, but we can already learn a ton from this announcement in its current form. Does Beijing want to hold back the tides of open models? Why is MOFCOM writing these rules now, and what does this say about the Chinese government’s appetite for AI-enabled risks versus growth? To find out, we spent three days poring over the draft regulations — so you don’t have to! What’s ahead: How these rules came to be — and how this draft is already affecting the Chinese AI industry; What the proposed rules mean for frontier models, chip design, memory, cybersecurity, AI content detection, and even China’s minority languages; Who actually decides which export licenses get approved, and the balance of power between provincial and central authorities; What these rules tell us about Beijing’s expectations for AI development. The 40 proposed additions in Announcement 48, split across AI, photovoltaics, and biomedicine. Today, we’re just focusing on the AI-related regulations, but a future piece tackling everything else — from this announcement’s proposed restrictions on PV cells and gene therapies, to other recent announcements on port dredgers and tunnel borers — is in the works! items.title: The Lithography Lever
items.content: Why should you care about lithography exports sold to China? What is Congress thinking about doing about it? And what does it mean for the future of humanity, the lightcone, great power relations — all of the above. Nick Brown is a co-founder of the Center for Technology and Statecraft (CTS) , a new think tank spun out of IFP, that looks at long-term technology challenges and opportunities facing the US. Nick was a physics major, spent a while as a software engineer in and around government, and had an arc as an aspiring concert violinist. But we’re here to talk about what is in pole position for my paper of the year: his master class on what would happen if the US cut off DUV exports to China: DUV Immersion Lithography: The Foundation of US AI Compute Advantage . Co-hosting is ChinaTalk’s Aqib Zakaria . We discuss: The case for banning DUV exports to China: Why lithography is the hardest part of the semiconductor manufacturing stack for China to replicate/indigenize and the strongest point of leverage the US and its allies have over China’s future AI compute. The cannonball-sized hole in US export controls: China imported roughly 90 immersion lithography systems a year in 2024–25, nearly two-thirds of ASML’s immersion exports. If imports continue at this rate, China could approach or even reach parity with the US in AI chipmaking within a decade. What the MATCH Act would do: How Congress could close this gap by restricting DUV immersion exports and servicing, and whether the US can get its allies on board. Will Beijing retaliate? Why a gradual, long-term restriction may be less likely to provoke another rare-earths crisis Buying time for AGI: How cutting off DUV imports could preserve America’s AI compute advantage into the 2030s, giving the US more time to navigate the technological, geopolitical, and societal implications of increasingly powerful AI. items.content: Almost 2 months ago, OpenAI introduced Daybreak for Frontline Defenders , a $1B subsidy for access to Daybreak cyber models and products. That funding came into use almost immediately, as major vulnerabilities in PHP were independently discovered by two parties: Ryan Austin, a researcher at the security firm Calif, as part of the OpenAI “ Patch the Planet ” project in August 2026 using GPT 5.6 Sol: View post on X … as well as Wiz, recently acquired into Google Cloud (using Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as their own tool, Wiz Atlas). All high profile cyber disclosures are at least a little bit of marketing, and the degree to which this was a severely alarming vulnerability on the order of famous ones like log4shell and Heartbleed is up to some debate , but surely the coordinated response across the PHP Ecosystem is the developer community responding in its most ideal form. We should expect to be in for at least a year of finding such critical vulnerabilities; but it is the wrong move to blame the messenger for finding them; rather it is good to know that our critical software is generally getting the biggest security audit it has ever had in human history. items.title: The Case for DUV Controls
items.content: Saif Khan makes his ChinaTalk debut. He is perhaps my favorite example of posting-to-policy that I’ve seen over the course of my time following Washington. Saif wrote some truly excellent deep dives into AI and semiconductors during his time at CSET, then went into the NSC and Commerce in the early-to-mid 2020s, across both the Biden and Trump II administrations, to help manifest the export control regulatory regime we have today. He is now out of government and launching the Center for Technology and Statecraft , an IFP -affiliated think tank, which is already producing excellent, grounded, technical, forward-looking work that will certainly shape many an AI policy discussion in the years to come. We discuss: Why Saif started a new think tank, and the value of deep, forward-looking policy research in an AI world moving at breakneck speed; CTS’s landmark DUV report, which projects that stopping tool exports today could leave China producing roughly 100x fewer AI chips than the US by the mid-2030s, making DUV controls the US’s most consequential lever over the AI balance; How rigorous research actually translates into government policy, and why think tank experience is valuable before working in government; Robotics as the next frontier of US-China AI competition, and the security vs. diffusion mindsets shaping AI policy; How AI is changing policy research itself, the challenge of bringing AI into government, and what AI-driven economic and social change could mean for humans. Plus, why everyone should read Lu Xun, why AI might socialize like insects, and AI-nannying. Listen now on your favorite podcast app ! Why Another Think Tank? Jordan Schneider: Saif Khan, at long last, welcome to ChinaTalk. Why does the world need another think tank? What is the appetite right now for evidence-based policy? items.title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust.  Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It…

items.title: Why a Chinese AI Lab’s Product Lead Thinks AGI is “Inevitable”
items.content: Richard Bian is the head of product operations for Ant Ling , the foundational LLM at Ant. If you don’t know Ant , they most famously make Alipay, which makes your money and your world run when you’re in China and sometimes beyond. Richard is a former software engineer at Microsoft and Square, and he previously served as head of open source at Ant, where he scaled the open source initiative into a dedicated team. He’s lived and worked in Singapore, Canada, the US, and China, and he loves to build products. Topics covered: ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. The Hugging Face hack as a sign of progress? Why Richard sees the incident involving OpenAI research agents as an inevitable discovery rather than simply a disaster, and why finding a solution now is a positive development. AGI is coming, but nobody knows what it will look like. AGI is inevitable, and we’re still in the early stages of figuring out what these models can do. Rather than obsessing over leaderboards, we need better evaluations and a more open-minded approach to judging models. Open source as a product strategy, not just a way to give things away. How open-weight models can harness global talent, accelerate development, and support a diverse ecosystem of products, and why the real business challenge is gross margins rather than capex. Why the AI conversation needs more voices. Why we need to pay attention to diverse perspectives on where AI is going, and be more willing to explore rather than declare the endgame. items.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
items.content: At a glance StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale  StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student  The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance  Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor  In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess,…

items.title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. items.title: 10 Takeaways from Q3
items.content: AI, China, defense, national security, supply chains, the Protestant roots of Kim Il-sung’s Messiah complex , the lethality of hydrofluoric acid, and horseback archery in Kyrgyzstan. It’s been a productive Q3. Here are some of the things we learned and why we think they matter. The ChinaTalk team is growing! We’ve welcomed Quinn Ennis , our newest full-time analyst, and Michael Palmer , who has been doing great work behind the scenes on video and audio! China and AI What does Liang Wenfeng actually believe? The DeepSeek Thesis reconstructs DeepSeek’s strategy from leaked minutes of a four-hour meeting between Liang Wenfeng and investors. For Liang, general intelligence is the only problem worth solving — products can wait, because “once truly generalized and convincingly superior intelligence arrives, creating to-C and to-B products will be trivial.” Why it matters: This is a rare window into the worldview of one of the most important people in Chinese AI. Liang is all-in on AGI rather than diverting focus toward commercializing current AI capabilities, and he’s betting that open models and Chinese chips can get him there. Why are Chinese AI researchers so skeptical of American AI safety? In How Chinese AI Radicalizes , Irene traces an unsettling development: some Chinese researchers are increasingly concluding that American AI-safety rhetoric is just a form of technological containment. DeepSeek researcher Liu Shengyu’s viral essay argues that frontier AI should be broadly accessible rather than controlled by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI (and yes, he mentions Hitler). In short, American AI safety rhetoric is backfiring in China. Why it matters: If Chinese AI researchers interpret American safety arguments through the lens of anti-China containment, genuine US-China cooperation becomes harder, just as increasingly capable AI makes cooperation more important. items.title: David Silver and Lasse Espeholt of Ineffable Intelligence: A Superlearner for the Age of Experience
items.content: Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:32 Collectively, you know, we started with this kind of gray mush in our head. We somehow started out knowing nothing at all and somehow discovered, like, everything that humans know today was, like, this process of collective discovery, like, of of languages and technology and science and mathematics and all the rest of it. Know, everything we learned, we discovered it for ourselves. And that's an incredible thing that no one has cracked yet in AI. And so to me, that is the essence of what it will take to get to superintelligence, like a system that can just keep learning and discovering knowledge forever. Speaker 2 | 00:49 - 01:10 I'm thrilled to have Dave Silver and Lesae Espeholt with us, two of the co founders of ineffable intelligence. Great name, by the way. Fun fact, Dave, you were the first person I cold emailed to come on training data when we started the show 100 ish episodes ago. And it feels like a full circle moment to finally have you on the show. So thank you for joining us. Speaker 1 | 01:11 - 01:11 Thank you. Speaker 2 | 01:12 - 01:43 Dave, let's start with you. Your 2009 PhD was on reinforcement learning applied to the devilishly difficult game of Go. You demonstrated for the world for the first time that superhuman in one domain machine intelligence was possible. And I think you were really the figure that inspired the entire current generation of reinforcement learning and deep learning researchers. And so thank you for your contributions to where the field is. Speaker 2 | 01:44 - 01:57 I'm curious, thinking back to that point in time, what did you learn? What did you have conviction on? And what has remained the same and what has changed as AI has changed over the last five years or so? Speaker 1 | 01:57 - 02:47 Yeah. Thank you, and pleasure to be here, and I'm glad I finally made it after these 100 episodes. It's a pleasure to be here. So I suppose I always had this conviction starting my PhD and going into the game of Go that the right approach to solve AI was through learning from experience, through systems that discovered things for themselves, that were learning through reinforcement learning to get better and better and better, and that that would be the thing which would lead to the emergence of intelligence and ultimately superintelligence. And so I suppose we were able to show that in the game of Go, but it's a conviction that has held true throughout my career, and here we are now applying that conviction, ineffable, trying to show that indeed superintelligence can emerge all the way through systems that learn from experience. Speaker 1 | 02:48 - 03:39 And in terms of things which are different, although we are not pursuing the human data path that the LLM world has pursued, I do think there's lots of interesting lessons to learn from that. In particular, it was definitely a surprise to me how a system that was trained on a massive amount of data could then be very quickly fine tuned on a very small amount of data to completely change its behavior. That was something which I think was something which changed my mindset in terms of just suggesting that if you get things at the right scale, that a lot of things which seem incredibly hard or they might be very slow, that once you've kind of experienced enough data, that after that, the things that were slow can become very fast. I think that's a lesson that wasn't obvious to me in advance until it happened. Speaker 2 | 03:39 - 03:56 Okay, we're going to come back to that later. You could have run this program inside DeepMind where could have probably had more access to compute than just about anybody. You decided the right thing to do was to start a new lab. Why'd you do that? Speaker 1 | 03:57 - 04:31 Yeah. So look, first of all, I had a fantastic time at DeepMind. items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.content: At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it. Growing our monorepo Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share…

items.title: China, the FCC, and the Logic of Transceivers
items.content: Quinn has joined the ChinaTalk team after studying semiconductor physics at Yale. Reach out to quinn@chinatalk.media to chat energy, BRI, robots, trade, industrial policy, or anything else! Over the past year, the FCC has released a series of restrictions on foreign-made hardware. First came drones, then routers, and then in July, inverters and robots. The newest devices to be considered are optical transceivers, which convert data into light and back within data centers. Following a Reuters report of a draft ban on new Chinese transceivers, markets responded as if it meant a straightforward substitution of supply, and American optics stocks rose while Chinese optics leaders fell. This swap is not that simple. The FCC’s cybersecurity logic is real but far narrower than the rule suggests. After explaining these gaps, I follow the transceiver supply chain from the module and the laser all the way down to the wafer and the metal it relies on. Chinese companies dominate the top of the stack but are reliant on Western companies in the middle. At the very bottom, Chinese control is ingrained, and the U.S.’s dependence on these basic materials will not be shifted by an FCC rule at the top of the stack. ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. The Rule On August 4, Reuters reported that the FCC was drafting a ban on import authorization for new models of Chinese optical transceivers to prevent Chinese firms from stealing data, installing malware, or disrupting service. Per the anonymous sources, officials want the rule published and effective by year end, though they cautioned the draft could still be modified or shelved. By the end of the week on August 7, Zhongji Innolight 中际旭创, the largest transceiver vendor globally, suffered a 10-percent drop in its stock price, while Coherent, a leading American transceiver manufacturer, saw its stock pri…

items.title: Building AI for Reliable Execution: Lessons From Industrial Robotics
items.content: When you think of robotics and AI, you probably first think of full humanoid robots like Figure’s AI-powered machines and 1X’s NEO home robots . Those may well be the future, but arguably more important in 2026 is industrial robots — which are typically not humanoids. Standard Bots claims to be “America’s largest AI-native industrial robot manufacturer.” It recently raised $200 million at a $1 billion valuation, in a series C round led by General Catalyst and RoboStrategy, a fund focused on robotics. Its customers include NASA, Amazon and Lockheed Martin. We spoke to Evan Beard , co-founder and CEO, and Leif Jentoft , Head of AI, to find out more about Standard Bots’ AI stack and how its models work. To set the scene, Standard Bots’ industrial robot arms are designed for tasks such as machine tending, welding, and assembly. Here’s a quick demo by Jentoft: Pretrained models and task-specific adaptation According to Beard, Standard Bots has a shared base model that customers adapt through demonstrations and fine-tuning. Jentoft added that Standard Bots runs a range of models , including a zero-shot perception system for machine tending. Beard says its largest model is in the low billions of parameters — so it’s not that large by frontier lab standards. “We believe data quality matters far more than raw volume,” said Jentoft, “and we focus on getting the most out of targeted data rather than chasing the largest possible dataset.” (This matches the “bitterest lesson” of Jev creator Diogo Almeida , who told us recently that the right task and the right data can matter more than compute.) “Our market access gives us unique access to the highest value data,” he added. “ In-situ interventions can fix an edge case with a few dozen examples.” Setting up part identification with ClickFind. Beard notes that Standard Bots focuses on short-horizon tasks t…
items.summary: Inside Standard Bots’ AI stack, pretrained models learn factory tasks from demonstrations and improve through corrections from real deployments.

items.title: Why AlphaFold Didn't Solve Protein Folding — Pushmeet Kohli, Google DeepMind & Sal Candido, Biohub
items.content: From the Bitter Lesson of AI scaling to the unsolved mysteries of protein folding , Google DeepMind’s Pushmeet Kohli and Biohub’s Sal Candido are rethinking what it takes to build AI that truly understands biology. In this special panel moderated by Brandon Anderson , they explore why AlphaFold’s breakthrough was only the beginning , why scaling compute and data alone won’t solve biology, and how the next generation of AI models could transform our understanding of proteins, cells, and human disease. We go deep on the future of AI-driven biology : finding scaling laws in biological data, the tradeoffs between scientific intuition and general-purpose architectures, why protein structure prediction is far from solved, and what it would take to build predictive models of living systems. Pushmeet reflects on the lessons behind AlphaFold , the limits of human interpretability, and whether future frontier models could understand other AI systems better than we can. Sal explains why protein language models may already contain scientific knowledge we haven’t unlocked, how biological modeling must move beyond individual proteins, and why achieving Biohub’s mission to cure all disease requires thinking in terms of 10x breakthroughs rather than incremental improvements. We discuss: The Bitter Lesson for biology : why scaling compute and data isn’t enough Why finding the right scaling law matters more than blindly increasing model size How low-quality metagenomic data can improve protein language models Why AI researchers optimize for available data instead of the most important scientific problems Lessons from DeepMind on balancing modeling, data generation, and scientific expertise Why building a virtual cell requires fundamentally different datasets AlphaFold’s handcrafted architecture and the role of scientific intuition Why good data matters more than simply having more data Inductive biases, scaling laws, and the future of…
items.summary: From the Bitter Lesson of AI scaling to the unsolved mysteries of protein folding, Google DeepMind’s Pushmeet Kohli and Biohub’s Sal Candido are rethinking what it takes to build AI that truly understands biology.
